definition: Computational creativity (also known as artificial creativity, mechanical creativity, creative computing or creative computation) is a multidisciplinary endeavour that is located at the intersection of the fields of artificial intelligence, cognitive psychology, philosophy, and the arts (e.g., computational art as part of computational culture).
details: Is the application of computer systems to emulate human-like creative processes, facilitating the generation of artistic and design outputs that mimic innovation and originality. The goal of computational creativity is to model, simulate or replicate creativity using a computer, to achieve one of several ends: To construct a program or computer capable of human-level creativity. To better understand human creativity and to formulate an algorithmic perspective on creative behavior in humans. To design programs that can enhance human creativity without necessarily being creative themselves. The field of computational creativity concerns itself with theoretical and practical issues in the study of creativity. Theoretical work on the nature and proper definition of creativity is performed in parallel with practical work on the implementation of systems that exhibit creativity, with one strand of work informing the other. The applied form of computational creativity is known as media synthesis.

explainer.lead: Computational creativity explores whether computers can produce things people experience as new and imaginative, and what that process reveals about human creativity. It covers both systems that generate art or designs and tools that help people create.

tiers.eli5: Imagine teaching a computer to brainstorm, much as you might invent a story or sketch a new kind of bicycle. The computer can suggest its own creations, or offer ideas that help you become more inventive. Researchers also use these experiments to learn how human creativity might work.
tiers.practitioner: Applications include systems that generate artistic or design outputs and interactive tools that supply options for people to select and refine. The intended role matters: a system may aim to emulate creativity, model human creative behaviour, or simply support a human creator. A polished output is not by itself evidence of human-level creativity, and a useful assistant need not be creative on its own.
tiers.paperLevel: Computational creativity is the computational modelling, simulation or replication of creativity, pursued at the intersection of artificial intelligence, cognitive psychology, philosophy and the arts. Its aims include human-level machine creativity, algorithmic accounts of human creative behaviour, and programs that enhance human creativity. Theoretical accounts and implemented systems inform one another, but defining creativity well enough to model and assess it remains a central problem.

explainer.example: A design program generates several unfamiliar layouts for a book cover. A designer selects one, adjusts its colours and typography, and uses the other suggestions to explore alternatives; the program enhances the designer’s creativity without having to demonstrate human-level creativity itself.

usedIn.name: Computational art
usedIn.detail: Computer systems generate artistic outputs within computational culture.

usedIn.name: Design
usedIn.detail: Programs produce candidate designs or help people explore and refine their own ideas.

usedIn.name: Media synthesis
usedIn.detail: The applied form of computational creativity, focused on producing creative media.

usedIn.name: Creativity research
usedIn.detail: Implemented systems provide a way to examine and model human creative behaviour algorithmically.

explainer.intuition: Creativity can be studied as a process rather than treated only as a mysterious human gift. By turning ideas about that process into programs, researchers can test them, generate new work, or build tools that expand what people can imagine.
howItWorks: Choose a goal: emulate creativity, explain human creativity, or assist a human creator.
Develop a theoretical account of the creative behaviour to be modelled.
Implement that account as a computer system that generates or supports creative work.
Examine the resulting artistic or design outputs for innovation and originality.
Use practical results to refine the theory and the system.
explainer.whyItMatters: The field connects the practical creation of art and design with deeper questions about what creativity is and whether it can be reproduced computationally. Its tools can support human creators while its models offer a way to investigate creative behaviour.
misconceptions: It is not only about building machines that replace human creators; assisting human creativity is also a central goal.
An output that looks original does not, on its own, establish that the system has human-level creativity.
The field is not purely engineering: definitions and theories of creativity develop alongside working systems.

diagram.caption: Theory and implementation inform each other, while systems either generate creative outputs or support human creators.
